readings.title: Young Night Thought
readings.challenge: Follow a parade that grows faster until it reaches a surprising place.
readings.focus: A child turns the dark before sleep into a grand procession that carries him off to the “town of Sleep.”
readings.context: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these poems from memories of his own childhood. Here a child lies in bed after the light goes out. Emperors and kings are rulers; a caravan is a long line of travellers. Read the first stanza steadily and let the last one speed up a little, as the marchers do.

excerpt.locator: IV, “Young Night Thought,” the complete poem; opens “ALL night long and every night, When my mamma puts out the light, I see the people…”; closes “…faster on they go, And still beside them close I keep Until we reach the town of Sleep.”.

questions.prompt: When does the child see the people marching by?
facilitatorNotes: Every night, after his mother puts out the light. He says he sees them “as plain as day,” even though the room is dark; ask what is strange about that.
evidence: When my mamma puts out the light,
As plain as day, before my eye.

questions.prompt: Who is in the parade? Name or act out some of the marchers.
facilitatorNotes: Armies, emperors, kings, and every kind of beast and man, like a circus. Any listed marcher counts; children may march, wave, or carry pretend things.
evidence: Armies and emperors and kings,
For every kind of beast and man

questions.prompt: Where does the march end, and what do you think the “town of Sleep” really is?
facilitatorNotes: The child keeps close beside the marchers until they reach the town of Sleep. A good reading is that he falls asleep while imagining the parade, so the march is his way of drifting off. A child who pictures a real dream town is also listening closely if they connect it with sleeping.
evidence: But still the faster on they go,
Until we reach the town of Sleep.

readings.title: Whole Duty of Children
readings.challenge: Hear three rules for children and the small joke that follows them.
readings.focus: A poem with a grand title gives a short list of good manners, then lets children off a little.
readings.context: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these poems from memories of his own childhood. A duty is something you ought to do; to behave mannerly means to have good manners. Read the first three lines like a grown-up giving rules, and the last line more softly.

excerpt.locator: V, “Whole Duty of Children,” the complete poem; opens “A CHILD should always say what's true And speak when he is spoken to, And behave mannerly…”; closes “…speak when he is spoken to, And behave mannerly at table; At least as far as he is able.”.

questions.prompt: What three things should a child always do, the poem says?
facilitatorNotes: Tell the truth, speak when spoken to, and have good manners at the table. Children can count them on their fingers.
evidence: A CHILD should always say what's true
And behave mannerly at table;

questions.prompt: “Speak when he is spoken to” is an old rule. What does it ask a child to do, and not to do?
facilitatorNotes: To answer when a grown-up speaks to you, and, in the old meaning, not to start talking or interrupt before then. Children may say whether they think that is a fair rule today.
evidence: And speak when he is spoken to,

questions.prompt: The last line says, “At least as far as he is able.” Is the poet being strict there, or kind?
facilitatorNotes: Kind, and a little funny: after a grand title, he admits a child can only do what a child is able to do. Some children may hear it as an excuse for not trying; the line allows both.
evidence: At least as far as he is able.

readings.title: Pirate Story
readings.challenge: Hear how three children turn a basket in a meadow into a ship at sea.
readings.focus: Pretend play changes ordinary things into a voyage, until real cows make the danger feel real.
readings.context: Three children sit in a basket by the swing and pretend it is a boat. A lea is a meadow; a squadron is a group of warships; a wicket is a small gate; a harbour is a safe place for boats. Africa, Providence, Babylon and Malabar are faraway places the children have heard of.

excerpt.locator: VII, “Pirate Story,” the complete poem; opens “THREE of us afloat in the meadow by the swing, Three of us aboard in the basket on the…”; closes “…they're as mad as they can be, The wicket is the harbour and the garden is the shore.”.

questions.prompt: What is the children’s “boat” really, and where is it?
facilitatorNotes: A basket in the meadow by the swing. The poem says they are “aboard,” but the place words show it is a game.
evidence: Three of us aboard in the basket on the lea.

questions.prompt: What makes the meadow look like the sea?
facilitatorNotes: The wind blows the long grass into waves. Children can show the moving grass with their hands.
evidence: And waves are on the meadow like the waves there are at sea.

questions.prompt: What is the “squadron” that charges at the children, and where do they escape to?
facilitatorNotes: The cattle in the meadow, which the children turn into an enemy fleet; the gate becomes their harbour and the garden their shore. Ask whether the children are truly frightened or enjoying the game; both readings can use “they're as mad as they can be.”
evidence: Cattle on the meadow a-charging with a roar!
The wicket is the harbour and the garden is the shore.

readings.title: Travel
readings.challenge: Picture a long list of faraway places, one after another.
readings.focus: A child who has only read about the world plans every place he will visit, and ends by imagining other children’s toys.
readings.context: The child in this poem has not been to these places; he knows them from books and pictures. Golden apples come from old stories; Crusoes are people shipwrecked alone, like Robinson Crusoe; a mosque is a Muslim place of worship and a minaret its tall tower; a bazaar is a market; a palanquin is a covered chair carried on poles; a caravan is a line of travellers with camels. Read it as one long breath of wishes. It is read on Columbus Day: in 1492 Christopher Columbus, too, sailed west hoping to reach the Eastern cities and China he knew from books, and landed instead on islands where the Taíno people already lived.
readings.contentNote: The poem names “negro hunters' huts,” an old word for Black African people, and pictures faraway lands as a Victorian child’s storybook showed them.

excerpt.locator: X, “Travel,” the complete poem; opens “I SHOULD like to rise and go Where the golden apples grow;-- Where below another sky…”; closes “…Heroes, fights and festivals; And in a corner find the toys Of the old Egyptian boys.”.

questions.prompt: Which animals does the child hope to see on his travels?
facilitatorNotes: Parrots, cockatoos and goats, apes, a crocodile, a red flamingo, tigers and camels. Children can choose one and act it out.
evidence: Where the knotty crocodile
And the red flamingo flies

questions.prompt: What is strange about the city in the desert?
facilitatorNotes: Nobody lives there any more: its children grew up long ago, there is not a foot in the streets, and no light at night. It is empty and still.
evidence: Not a stir of child or mouse,
In all the town no spark of light.

questions.prompt: When he gets there as a man, what will he find in a corner? Why might he look for that?
facilitatorNotes: The toys of the old Egyptian boys. After all the grand places, he still thinks about children like himself who played long ago. Children may say he wants to play with them, or wonders who owned them; both fit.
evidence: And in a corner find the toys
Of the old Egyptian boys.

readings.title: Looking Forward
readings.challenge: Notice the gap between what a child plans to be and what he plans to do.
readings.focus: A child imagines being grown up, proud and great, and plans to use all that greatness to guard his toys.
readings.context: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these poems as if a child were speaking. Man's estate means being a grown man; to meddle with something means to touch it or interfere with it when it is not yours.

excerpt.locator: XII, “Looking Forward,” the complete poem; opens “WHEN I am grown to man's estate I shall be very proud and great. And tell the other girls…”; closes “…be very proud and great. And tell the other girls and boys Not to meddle with my toys.”.

questions.prompt: What will the child be like when he is grown up?
facilitatorNotes: Very proud and great: important, and pleased with himself.
evidence: I shall be very proud and great.

questions.prompt: What is the first thing he plans to tell the other girls and boys?
facilitatorNotes: Not to meddle with his toys.
evidence: And tell the other girls and boys
Not to meddle with my toys.

questions.prompt: Would a real grown-up worry most about toys? What makes this poem funny?
facilitatorNotes: The child imagines being great but still cares most about what a child cares about. That is the joke: he plans to be grown up and still sounds just like a child. Some children may answer that grown-ups guard their things too, which is also true.
evidence: WHEN I am grown to man's estate
Not to meddle with my toys.

readings.title: The Land of Nod
readings.challenge: Compare where the child goes by day with where he goes at night.
readings.focus: Dreams become a faraway land the child must visit alone and cannot find again by day.
readings.context: “Nod” is an old joke name for sleep, from nodding off. Abroad here means away from home; afar means far away; curious means strange.

excerpt.locator: XVII, “The Land of Nod,” the complete poem; opens “FROM breakfast on through all the day At home among my friends I stay; But every night I…”; closes “…can get back by day, Nor can remember plain and clear The curious music that I hear.”.

questions.prompt: Where does the child stay all day, and where does he go every night?
facilitatorNotes: At home with his friends by day; far away in the land of Nod at night. The first stanza is built on this contrast between day and night.
evidence: At home among my friends I stay;
Afar into the land of Nod.

questions.prompt: Who goes with him to the land of Nod?
facilitatorNotes: No one: he goes all by himself, with nobody to tell him what to do. Some children will find that lonely and some exciting; let them choose and point to the line.
evidence: All by myself I have to go,
With none to tell me what to do--

questions.prompt: Why can’t he find the way back in the daytime? What is the land of Nod really?
facilitatorNotes: It is the land of dreams, which vanish on waking; he cannot even remember the music clearly. Children may connect this with forgetting their own dreams.
evidence: I never can get back by day,
The curious music that I hear.

readings.title: System
readings.challenge: Follow a child’s rule about who is good and who is naughty, and test whether it works.
readings.focus: A child decides that good children are clean, neat and rewarded, then finds he must explain a child who is not.
readings.context: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these poems as if a child were speaking. A system is a fixed way of doing things. In Stevenson’s time an orange was a special treat for a child. Papa means father. Read the second stanza slowly; its last line changes what the child has been saying.

excerpt.locator: XIX, “System,” the complete poem; opens “EVERY night my prayers I say, And get my dinner every day; And every day that I've been…”; closes “…toys and things to eat, He is a naughty child, I'm sure-- Or else his dear papa is poor.”.

questions.prompt: What does the child get on every day that he has been good?
facilitatorNotes: An orange after his meal.
evidence: I get an orange after food.

questions.prompt: The child says another child must be naughty. Which child does he mean?
facilitatorNotes: A child who is not clean and neat and does not have lots of toys and things to eat. He is sure such a child is naughty.
evidence: The child that is not clean and neat,
He is a naughty child, I'm sure--

questions.prompt: Then he adds, “Or else his dear papa is poor.” What has he started to notice? Is his system fair?
facilitatorNotes: That a child may lack toys and food because the family is poor, not because the child is bad. Many children will say the system is unfair; others may say the speaker is beginning to understand. Both can use the last line.
evidence: Or else his dear papa is poor.

readings.title: A Good Boy
readings.challenge: Hear how a whole happy day leads to a peaceful bedtime.
readings.focus: A child who knows he has been good feels sure his sleep will be calm and his morning bright.
readings.context: “Sleepsin-by” is a baby word for going to sleep. Linen is the cloth of bed sheets; fair here means clean and pale. Thrushes are songbirds, and lilacs are bushes with sweet-smelling flowers.

excerpt.locator: XX, “A Good Boy,” the complete poem; opens “I WOKE before the morning, I was happy all the day, I never said an ugly word, but smiled…”; closes “…till I waken in the dawn, And hear the thrushes singing in the lilacs round the lawn.”.

questions.prompt: What did the boy do all day to be good?
facilitatorNotes: He never said an ugly word, smiled, and kept on playing. He was happy all day long.
evidence: I never said an ugly word, but smiled and stuck to play.

questions.prompt: How does his bed seem to him tonight?
facilitatorNotes: Cool, fresh and smooth, as if it were waiting for him. Ask the child to describe their own bed with one of these words.
evidence: My bed is waiting cool and fresh, with linen smooth and fair,

questions.prompt: Why is the boy sure no ugly dream will frighten him? Do you think being good keeps bad dreams away?
facilitatorNotes: He feels happy because he knows he has been good, so he expects to sleep tight until the thrushes sing. Some children will agree; others may say anyone can have a bad dream. The poem tells how the boy feels, not a rule.
evidence: And I am very happy, for I know that I've been good.
No ugly dream shall fright my mind, no ugly sight my eyes,

readings.title: Escape at Bedtime
readings.challenge: Picture a sky full of stars and listen for the things the child compares them with.
readings.focus: A child who slips outside at bedtime is so dazzled by the stars that they keep shining in his head after he is caught.
readings.context: The child has slipped out of the house when he should be going to bed. The Dog, the Plough and the Hunter are names of star pictures, or constellations; the Star of the Sailor is the North Star, which sailors steered by. Ne'er means never.

excerpt.locator: XXI, “Escape at Bedtime,” the complete poem; opens “THE lights from the parlour and kitchen shone out Through the blinds and the windows and…”; closes “…But the glory kept shining and bright in my eyes, And the stars going round in my head.”.

questions.prompt: The stars are more than what? Find one thing the child compares them with.
facilitatorNotes: More than the leaves on a tree, or the people in church or the park. Any one comparison is enough; the point is that there are too many stars to count.
evidence: There ne'er were such thousands of leaves on a tree,
Nor of people in church or the Park,

questions.prompt: Where else does the child see stars besides the sky?
facilitatorNotes: In the pail by the wall, half full of water that reflects them. Ask how water can “hold” stars.
evidence: Would be half full of water and stars.

questions.prompt: Who are “they” who chase him, and what can’t they take away from him?
facilitatorNotes: Probably the grown-ups of the house, who pack him into bed. They can put him to bed, but the glory of the stars keeps shining in his eyes and head. Some children think he is in trouble, others that he is happy; the last lines support both.
evidence: And they soon had me packed into bed;
And the stars going round in my head.

readings.title: Marching Song
readings.challenge: Keep time with a pretend parade and notice who has each job.
readings.focus: Children make a grand army out of a comb, a drum and a napkin, then cheerfully march home again.
readings.context: Children play at soldiers. To play upon a comb, you hum against paper wrapped round a comb. A highland bonnet is a Scottish cap; a Grenadier is a soldier; martial means soldierly. Fame and pillage, glory and plunder, are words from real wars used here in fun. Read with a marching beat.

excerpt.locator: XXII, “Marching Song,” the complete poem; opens “BRING the comb and play upon it! Marching, here we come! Willie cocks his highland…”; closes “…Great commander Jane! Now that we've been round the village, Let's go home again.”.

questions.prompt: What does Johnnie do, and what does Mary Jane do?
facilitatorNotes: Johnnie beats the drum and Mary Jane commands the party. Children can act out one of the jobs, or Willie’s or Peter’s.
evidence: Johnnie beats the drum.
Mary Jane commands the party,

questions.prompt: What do the children use for a flag?
facilitatorNotes: A napkin waving on a stick. The poem shows play turning household things into an army’s gear.
evidence: While the napkin like a banner
Waves upon the stick!

questions.prompt: How far does the army march, and why do you think they go home?
facilitatorNotes: Round the village. They may be tired, hungry, or simply finished with the game; the poem calls it “enough of fame,” as if the adventure were complete. Accept any reason tied to the last stanza.
evidence: Now that we've been round the village,
Let's go home again.

readings.title: The Cow
readings.challenge: Notice everything the cow does in the open air.
readings.focus: A child thanks a cow for her cream and pictures her calm and free in the meadow.
readings.context: Lowing is the soft sound a cow makes. To stray is to wander off and get lost. Cream is the rich top of fresh milk.

excerpt.locator: XXIII, “The Cow,” the complete poem; opens “THE friendly cow all red and white, I love with all my heart: She gives me cream with all…”; closes “…wet with all the showers, She walks among the meadow grass And eats the meadow flowers.”.

questions.prompt: What does the cow give the child, and what does he eat it with?
facilitatorNotes: Cream, to eat with apple tart. The child’s love begins with a treat.
evidence: She gives me cream with all her might,
To eat with apple-tart.

questions.prompt: The cow wanders “here and there,” yet “cannot stray.” How can both be true?
facilitatorNotes: She can roam about her field, but a hedge or fence keeps her from getting lost. Children may offer other answers, such as that she always comes home; accept them if they explain both lines.
evidence: She wanders lowing here and there,
And yet she cannot stray,

questions.prompt: What weather does the cow meet in the last stanza? Do you think she minds it?
facilitatorNotes: Wind and showers. She simply walks and eats the meadow flowers, so she seems calm; a child who says being wet would bother them is making a fair comparison with themselves.
evidence: And blown by all the winds that pass
And wet with all the showers,

readings.title: Keepsake Mill
readings.challenge: Follow two friends to a secret place, then forward to when they are grown up.
readings.focus: A noisy mill by the river becomes the place where old friends promise to meet and remember.
readings.context: A mill uses a big wheel turned by the river to grind grain into flour. A weir is a low wall across a river; the sluice and the race are channels that carry water to the wheel; moil means noisy work. A keepsake is something you keep to remember someone. Children were not allowed out over the garden wall, so the poem jokes that it is “a sin without pardon.”

excerpt.locator: XXVI, “Keepsake Mill,” the complete poem; opens “OVER the borders, a sin without pardon, Breaking the branches and crawling below, Out…”; closes “…Honoured and old and all gaily apparelled, Here we shall meet and remember the past.”.

questions.prompt: How do the children get out of the garden? Are they allowed to?
facilitatorNotes: They break through the branches, crawl under, and go out through a gap in the wall. Calling it “a sin without pardon” shows they know it is not allowed, said with a grin.
evidence: OVER the borders, a sin without pardon,
Out through the breach in the wall of the garden,

questions.prompt: What sounds and sights make the mill a marvellous place?
facilitatorNotes: The mill hums like thunder, the weir foams, the water races under the sluice. Let the child make the mill’s sound.
evidence: Here is the mill with the humming of thunder,
Here is the weir with the wonder of foam,

questions.prompt: When the two friends meet again as grown-ups, what will each bring? Why those things?
facilitatorNotes: The bean and the marble they gave each other after a quarrel: keepsakes of their friendship. Like the wheel that keeps turning, their friendship will still be there. Children may also notice the quarrel did not end the friendship.
evidence: You with the bean that I gave when we quarrelled,
Here we shall meet and remember the past.

readings.title: Good and Bad Children
readings.challenge: Listen for when a poem is giving advice and when it is joking.
readings.focus: Grown-up warnings to children are made so big and rhyming that they become funny.
readings.context: The poem speaks to children like a solemn grown-up, but it is partly teasing. Brittle means easily broken; sedately means slowly and calmly; diet means food; sages are wise people; unduly means too much; gabies is an old word for silly people.

excerpt.locator: XXVII, “Good and Bad Children,” the complete poem; opens “CHILDREN, you are very little, And your bones are very brittle; If you would grow great…”; closes “…up as geese and gabies, Hated, as their age increases, By their nephews and their nieces.”.

questions.prompt: What does the poem tell little children to do if they want to grow up great?
facilitatorNotes: Walk sedately, be bright and quiet, eat simple food, and stay innocent and honest. Children can show what walking sedately looks like.
evidence: You must try to walk sedately.
And content with simple diet;

questions.prompt: How did children long ago grow into kings and wise people, the poem says?
facilitatorNotes: With happy hearts and faces and happy play in grassy places. Notice that this advice is about being happy and playing, not only about being quiet.
evidence: Happy play in grassy places--
Children grew to kings and sages.

questions.prompt: What does the poem say happens to cruel children? Do you think the poem is serious, or teasing?
facilitatorNotes: They grow up as geese and gabies, disliked by their own nephews and nieces. The silly rhymes and the strange punishment suggest Stevenson is laughing at grown-up warnings; a child who hears real advice about kindness is also right.
evidence: All grow up as geese and gabies,
By their nephews and their nieces.

readings.title: Foreign Children
readings.challenge: Notice what the speaker thinks of himself, and decide whether you agree.
readings.focus: A child at home in Britain boasts to children of faraway lands that his own life is best, and the poem lets readers smile at him.
readings.context: The speaker is a British child of long ago. Indian here means a Native American; the Sioux and the Crow are Native American nations; Eskimo is an old outside name for Arctic peoples such as the Inuit; a Turk comes from Turkey; “Japanee” is the child’s own word for Japanese. Stevenson himself loved travel and lived far from home.
readings.contentNote: The speaking child uses old names for peoples (“Indian,” “Eskimo,” “Japanee”) and says his own food and home are better than other children’s; the poem shows a narrow child’s view rather than recommending it.

excerpt.locator: XXVIII, “Foreign Children,” the complete poem; opens “LITTLE Indian, Sioux or Crow, Little frosty Eskimo, Little Turk or Japanee, O! don't you…”; closes “…Crow, Little frosty Eskimo, Little Turk or Japanee, O! don't you wish that you were me?”.

questions.prompt: Which children does the speaker talk to?
facilitatorNotes: A Native American child, an Arctic child, a Turkish child and a Japanese child, named in his old-fashioned words.
evidence: LITTLE Indian, Sioux or Crow,
Little Turk or Japanee,

questions.prompt: What exciting things does he say the other children have seen and done?
facilitatorNotes: Seen scarlet trees and lions, eaten ostrich eggs, and turned turtles over. Ask whether those sound dull or exciting.
evidence: And the lions over seas;
You have eaten ostrich eggs,

questions.prompt: He asks, “don't you wish that you were me?” What might the other children answer? Is he right?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks his own home and “proper meat” are best, but the other children would probably love their own homes and food just as much. The poem lets us smile at someone who thinks his way is the only right one; children may also say it is fine to love your own home.
evidence: But it's not so nice as mine:
I am fed on proper meat;

readings.title: The Sun’s Travels
readings.challenge: Imagine two places on the earth at the same moment.
readings.focus: When it is bedtime for one child, the sun is making morning for children far away.
readings.context: “Indian” here means children in India, far to the east of Britain; “the children in the West” are across the Atlantic Ocean, in America. The poem says the sun goes round the earth, as it seems to; really the earth turns. A lamp and a ball can show day and night.

excerpt.locator: XXIX, “The Sun's Travels,” the complete poem; opens “THE sun is not a-bed, when I At night upon my pillow lie; Still round the earth his way…”; closes “…the Atlantic Sea, And all the children in the West Are getting up and being dressed.”.

questions.prompt: Where is the sun when the child lies in bed at night?
facilitatorNotes: Not in bed: it is still travelling, making morning somewhere else. The first line answers a child’s question about where the sun goes.
evidence: THE sun is not a-bed, when I
Still round the earth his way he takes,

questions.prompt: What are children in India doing while this child plays in the sunny garden?
facilitatorNotes: Being kissed and put to bed. The poem pairs each scene with its opposite.
evidence: Is being kissed and put to bed.

questions.prompt: Why are children in the West getting up just when this child rises from tea?
facilitatorNotes: Because the day is only now dawning across the Atlantic. Two hands or a lamp and a ball can show that morning reaches different places at different times; children need not explain the whole earth.
evidence: Day dawns beyond the Atlantic Sea,
Are getting up and being dressed.

readings.title: The Lamplighter
readings.challenge: Hear what the child wants to be when he grows up and compare it with the others’ wishes.
readings.focus: A child admires the man who lights the street lamps and asks him for one small kindness.
readings.context: Before electric streetlights, a lamplighter walked through town each evening with a ladder and a flame to light the gas lamps. Leerie is the child’s name for him. Posting means hurrying; tea is the early evening meal; a banker looks after money. It is read on Labor Day, a holiday for the people whose work keeps a town going.

excerpt.locator: XXX, “The Lamplighter,” the complete poem; opens “MY tea is nearly ready and the sun has left the sky; It's time to take the window to see…”; closes “…by with ladder and with light, O Leerie, see a little child and nod to him to-night!”.

questions.prompt: What does Leerie carry as he comes up the street?
facilitatorNotes: A lantern and a ladder, so he can climb to each lamp and light it.
evidence: With lantern and with ladder he comes posting up the street.

questions.prompt: Tom wants to be a driver and Maria wants to go to sea. What does this child want to do?
facilitatorNotes: Go round at night lighting the lamps with Leerie. Ask why that might seem better to him than being rich like Papa; children may mention the light, the ladder, or being out after dark.
evidence: O Leerie, I'll go round at night and light the lamps with you!

questions.prompt: What does the child ask Leerie to do at the very end, and why might it matter so much?
facilitatorNotes: To notice a little child and nod to him. He wants someone he admires to see him; some children will say he wants to be Leerie’s friend.
evidence: O Leerie, see a little child and nod to him to-night!

readings.title: The Moon
readings.challenge: Sort creatures into those that love the night and those that belong to the day.
readings.focus: The moon shines on everyone, but only the creatures of the night come out to enjoy her.
readings.context: Harbour quays are where boats tie up. A bat sleeps through the day and flies at night. Read the noisy middle stanza with its squalls and howls, then the last stanza softly.

excerpt.locator: XXXII, “The Moon,” the complete poem; opens “THE moon has a face like the clock in the hall; She shines on thieves on the garden wall,…”; closes “…And flowers and children close their eyes Till up in the morning the sun shall arise.”.

questions.prompt: What does the moon’s face look like, according to the first line?
facilitatorNotes: The clock in the hall. A round, pale face fits both.
evidence: THE moon has a face like the clock in the hall;

questions.prompt: Which animals love to be out by the light of the moon?
facilitatorNotes: The cat, the mouse, the dog and the bat. Children can make one of their sounds.
evidence: The squalling cat and the squeaking mouse,
All love to be out by the light of the moon.

questions.prompt: Who hides from the moon, and when will they wake?
facilitatorNotes: The things that belong to the day, flowers and children among them, cuddle to sleep until the sun rises. Ask whether the listener is a day thing or a night thing.
evidence: Cuddle to sleep to be out of her way;
Till up in the morning the sun shall arise.

readings.title: Time to Rise
readings.challenge: Hear a tiny scene and the joke at its end.
readings.focus: A bird plays the part of a grown-up waking a lazy child.
readings.context: A window sill is the ledge under a window. 'Shamed means ashamed; a sleepy-head is someone who will not get up. Read the bird’s question in a cheeky voice.

excerpt.locator: XXXIV, “Time to Rise,” the complete poem; opens “A BIRDIE with a yellow bill Hopped upon the window sill, Cocked his shining eye and said:…”; closes “…the window sill, Cocked his shining eye and said: 'Ain't you 'shamed, you sleepy-head?'”.

questions.prompt: Where does the birdie hop?
facilitatorNotes: Onto the window sill, where the child in bed can see him.
evidence: Hopped upon the window sill,

questions.prompt: What does the bird look like? Find two details.
facilitatorNotes: A yellow bill and a shining eye, which he cocks, or tilts. Children can show the head tilt.
evidence: A BIRDIE with a yellow bill
Cocked his shining eye and said:

questions.prompt: Who is the sleepy-head, and why is it funny that a bird asks the question?
facilitatorNotes: The child still in bed. Birds are up at dawn, so this one can tease; usually a grown-up would say it. Accept other ideas about the joke.
evidence: 'Ain't you 'shamed, you sleepy-head?'

readings.title: North-West Passage
readings.challenge: Follow a child’s trip from the fireside to his bed in three short parts.
readings.focus: Going up a dark staircase to bed becomes a brave voyage, with shadows for enemies and the bedroom for a safe harbour.
readings.context: The North-West Passage was a sea route through the icy north that explorers searched for, braving cold and danger; Stevenson gives that name to a child’s trip up a dark passage to bed. Embers are glowing bits of the fire; undaunted means not afraid; sire is an old word for father; the Bogie is a make-believe night monster; balusters are the posts of the stair rail; a port is a harbour where ships are safe; the Land of Nod is sleep. Read “Shadow March” with a steady “tramp, tramp, tramp.”

excerpt.locator: XLI, “North-West Passage,” the complete poem in three parts: “Good Night,” “Shadow March” and “In Port”; opens “When the bright lamp is carried in, The sunless hours again begin; O'er all without, in…”; closes “…in with tip-toe tread, And see me lying warm and fast And in the Land of Nod at last.”.

questions.prompt: In the first part, to whom does the child say goodnight?
facilitatorNotes: His brother, his sister and his father, and the whole “pleasant party round the fire,” with its songs and tales.
evidence: Farewell, O brother, sister, sire!

questions.prompt: What are the “wicked shadows” on the stairs really the shadows of? Does knowing that make them less scary?
facilitatorNotes: The stair posts, the lamp, and the child himself. Some children will say yes, they are only shadows; others will say they still feel scary in the dark, as his drumming heart shows.
evidence: The shadow of the balusters, the shadow of the lamp,
The shadow of the child that goes to bed--

questions.prompt: Why is the last part called “In Port”? What makes the bedroom safe?
facilitatorNotes: A port is where a ship is safe after a voyage. His room is warm and cheerful, the door shuts the shadows out, and his mother looks in on him as he sleeps. Children may name any of these.
evidence: Into my warm and cheerful room.
And close the happy door at last

readings.title: The Unseen Playmate
readings.challenge: Collect clues about someone nobody has ever seen.
readings.focus: When a child plays happily alone, an invisible friend seems to join in and even look after the toys at night.
readings.context: Laurels are thick bushes; a musical glass is a glass that rings when you tap it. Soldiers of tin are toy soldiers; in old games British children played battles against the French, and the playmate always takes the losing side.

excerpt.locator: The Child Alone, I, “The Unseen Playmate,” the complete poem; opens “WHEN children are playing alone on the green, In comes the playmate that never was seen.…”; closes “…they're lying, in cupboard or shelf, 'Tis he will take care of your playthings himself!”.

questions.prompt: When does the Friend of the Children come?
facilitatorNotes: When children are playing alone, happy and good. He never comes to a crowd.
evidence: children are playing alone on the green,
When children are happy and lonely and good,

questions.prompt: Has anyone ever seen the playmate? Where does he like to be?
facilitatorNotes: Nobody has seen or heard him, and you could not draw him. He lies in the laurels, runs on the grass, and lives in the caves you dig.
evidence: Nobody heard him and nobody saw,
He lies in the laurels, he runs on the grass,

questions.prompt: Who do you think the unseen playmate really is?
facilitatorNotes: Many readers think he is the child’s own imagination, since he does just what the child is doing: digging, singing, playing soldiers. Others may picture a real fairy friend. Either can use the clue that he takes care of the toys.
evidence: His is a picture you never could draw,
'Tis he will take care of your playthings himself!

readings.title: My Ship and I
readings.challenge: Tell the difference between what happens now and what the child plans for later.
readings.focus: A boy whose toy boat only turns in circles on a pond dreams of shrinking to sail it to an island.
readings.context: The ship is a toy boat on a pond. The helm is where a ship is steered, and the dolly at the helm is a toy sailor. The prow and the bow are the front of a boat. “Divie-divie dive” is a made-up sound for a boat dipping through waves. A penny cannon is a tiny toy cannon.

excerpt.locator: The Child Alone, II, “My Ship and I,” the complete poem; opens “O IT'S I that am the captain of a tidy little ship, Of a ship that goes a-sailing on the…”; closes “…land upon the island where no dolly was before, And to fire the penny cannon in the bow.”.

questions.prompt: Where does the captain’s ship sail now, and what does it keep doing?
facilitatorNotes: On the pond, where it keeps turning round and round. He has not yet found out how to send it farther.
evidence: Of a ship that goes a-sailing on the pond;
And my ship it keeps a-turning all around and all about;

questions.prompt: What is the boy’s plan for sailing far away?
facilitatorNotes: To grow as little as the toy sailor and make the dolly come alive to help him sail. Ask whether that could really happen; it is a wish, said as if it were a plan.
evidence: For I mean to grow as little as the dolly at the helm,
And the dolly I intend to come alive;

questions.prompt: What will he do when he reaches the island? Why does he want to be first?
facilitatorNotes: Land where no dolly has ever been and fire his penny cannon. He wants to be an explorer who finds a new place. Children may pick another reason, such as adventure or being brave.
evidence: To land upon the island where no dolly was before,
And to fire the penny cannon in the bow.

readings.title: Picture-Books in Winter
readings.challenge: Find what winter takes away and where the child finds it again.
readings.focus: Picture books keep summer’s pretty things for children through the cold months.
readings.context: Rooks are big black birds; robins come close to windows in winter. Crooks are shepherds’ hooked sticks. A nursery nook is a cosy corner of a children’s room, and chimney-corner days are days spent by the fire.

excerpt.locator: The Child Alone, IV, “Picture-Books in Winter,” the complete poem; opens “SUMMER fading, winter comes-- Frosty mornings, tingling thumbs, Window robins, winter…”; closes “…Happy chimney-corner days, Sitting safe in nursery nooks, Reading picture story-books?”.

questions.prompt: What tells the child that winter has come?
facilitatorNotes: Frosty mornings, tingling thumbs, robins at the window and rooks. Children can add a sign of winter of their own, kept separate from the poem’s.
evidence: Frosty mornings, tingling thumbs,
Window robins, winter rooks,

questions.prompt: What has happened to the water, and where can the child still find flowing brooks?
facilitatorNotes: It has frozen hard as stone, so he and Nurse can walk on it; the flowing brooks are still in the picture books.
evidence: Water now is turned to stone
Still we find the flowing brooks

questions.prompt: Every stanza ends with the picture story-books. Why do you think the poet keeps coming back to them?
facilitatorNotes: The books are where every good thing in the poem is kept, so each stanza leads back to them, and the last asks how to praise them. Some children will simply enjoy the echo, which is part of the answer too.
evidence: In the picture story-books.
Reading picture story-books?

readings.title: My Treasures
readings.challenge: Listen to a list of treasures and the story that goes with each one.
readings.focus: Ordinary things become treasures because of where they were found, who made them, and what the child believes about them.
readings.context: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these poems as if a child were speaking. Nursie is the nurse who looked after him. A plane is a kind of tree; a chisel is a carpenter’s tool with a sharp blade for shaping wood. Let the child count the treasures on fingers as you read.

excerpt.locator: The Child Alone, V, “My Treasures,” the complete poem; opens “THESE nuts, that I keep in the back of the nest Where all my lead soldiers are lying at…”; closes “…And that is a chisel, both handle and blade, Which a man who was really a carpenter made.”.

questions.prompt: Name the child’s four treasures.
facilitatorNotes: Nuts, a whistle, a coloured stone, and a chisel.
evidence: THESE nuts, that I keep in the back of the nest
And that is a chisel, both handle and blade,

questions.prompt: The child is sure his stone is gold. What does his father say? Why might it still be a treasure?
facilitatorNotes: His father says it is not gold. It is still precious because the child found it far away and carried it home though he was tired and cold. Some children may believe it really is gold; the poem only gives the child’s word against his father’s.
evidence: For though father denies it, I'm sure it is gold.
And I carried it back although weary and cold,

questions.prompt: Why is the chisel “the king” of all his treasures? Which would you choose?
facilitatorNotes: Few children own one, and a real carpenter made it, so it is a grown-up’s tool. A child may choose the whistle instead, because nursie made it; any choice with a reason from the poem works.
evidence: But of all of my treasures the last is the king,
Which a man who was really a carpenter made.

readings.title: The Land of Story-Books
readings.challenge: See one room in two ways: as a parlour and as a wild land.
readings.focus: Behind the sofa, a child plays the adventure books he has read, until bedtime calls him home.
readings.context: In the evening the parents sit by the fire while the child crawls off with a toy gun. Solitudes are lonely places; a brink is an edge; a scout is someone who creeps close to spy. The Indian scout comes from the adventure books the boy has read.

excerpt.locator: The Child Alone, VII, “The Land of Story-Books,” the complete poem; opens “AT evening when the lamp is lit, Around the fire my parents sit; They sit at home and…”; closes “…return across the sea, And go to bed with backward looks At my dear land of Story-books.”.

questions.prompt: What are the parents doing while the child plays?
facilitatorNotes: Sitting by the fire, talking and singing. The child notices that they “do not play at anything.”
evidence: Around the fire my parents sit;
And do not play at anything.

questions.prompt: What is the forest track really? What are the hills and the woods?
facilitatorNotes: The dark space along the wall and behind the sofa. The room itself becomes hills, woods and a river in his game.
evidence: Away behind the sofa back.
These are the hills, these are the woods,

questions.prompt: How does the boy feel when his nurse comes to take him to bed? How do you know?
facilitatorNotes: Sorry to leave: he goes with “backward looks” at his dear land. He returns “across the sea” as if coming home from a long trip. Ask what game the child would be sad to leave.
evidence: Home I return across the sea,
And go to bed with backward looks

readings.title: Armies in the Fire
readings.challenge: Picture shapes that appear in a fire, fade, and come back.
readings.focus: At dusk a child stares into the glowing coals and sees burning cities and marching armies.
readings.context: Before electric heating, rooms were warmed by coal fires, and children liked to stare into the glowing coals and see pictures there. Even means evening; gloom means darkness; a spire is the pointed top of a church tower; lustre means shine; a phantom is something you seem to see that is not really there; embers are the glowing bits of the fire; a furnace is a very hot fire.

excerpt.locator: The Child Alone, VIII, “Armies in the Fire,” the complete poem; opens “THE lamps now glitter down the street; Faintly sound the falling feet; And the blue even…”; closes “…those armies marching to, And what the burning city is That crumbles in your furnaces!”.

questions.prompt: What time of day is it when the poem begins? What tells you?
facilitatorNotes: Evening: the street lamps are lit and the blue evening is falling over the garden.
evidence: THE lamps now glitter down the street;
And the blue even slowly falls

questions.prompt: What does the child see in the fire, and what happens to it?
facilitatorNotes: Armies marching past the towers of a burning city. They fade as the fire dies down, then come back when the glow returns.
evidence: Armies march by tower and spire
The armies fade, the lustre dies.

questions.prompt: At the end the child asks the embers questions. Can they answer? Why does he ask anyway?
facilitatorNotes: No, they are only coals. He wants to know the rest of the story his eyes have made up, so he asks as if the fire could tell him. Children may say he is half asleep or playing; both fit the dark, quiet room.
evidence: Blinking embers, tell me true
Where are those armies marching to,

readings.title: Night and Day
readings.challenge: Follow the garden from evening, through the night, to morning.
readings.focus: The garden seems to vanish at night with the child and returns with the morning to call him out to play.
readings.context: A portal is a doorway. Mortal things are living things; here the poem means everything in the garden. Whins are prickly bushes; lumber is old stored things; even is evening; a glade is an open grassy space; allies are friends on your side. A maid was a servant who opened the house each morning.

excerpt.locator: Garden Days, I, “Night and Day,” the complete poem; opens “WHEN the golden day is done, Through the closing portal, Child and garden, flower and…”; closes “…come On the smiling valleys; We have beat the morning drum; Playmate, join your allies!"”.

questions.prompt: What vanishes when the golden day is done?
facilitatorNotes: The child and the garden, the flowers and the sun: everything disappears into the dark.
evidence: Child and garden, flower and sun,

questions.prompt: Who is still awake in the dark while the child sleeps?
facilitatorNotes: A glow-worm in the road, mice among old things, and the parents moving with candles.
evidence: Glow-worm in the highway rut,
Parents move with candles;

questions.prompt: In the morning, who calls the child, and what do they say? Why might the garden call him a playmate?
facilitatorNotes: The paths, the roses and the forget-me-nots cry “Up!” and say they have beaten the morning drum. The garden is like a friend who has been waiting all night to play; children may hear soldiers calling a friend to join them.
evidence: We have beat the morning drum;
Playmate, join your allies!

readings.title: Nest Eggs
readings.challenge: Hold a before-and-after picture in mind: eggs now, flying birds soon.
readings.focus: Children watching a nest realize that the tiny birds will soon do what children never can.
readings.context: An arbour is a shady shelter of leaves; the laurel is a bushy evergreen; gabies are silly people who stare; frail means easily broken. Children of Stevenson’s time often looked into wild nests. Today wild birds’ nests and eggs are protected by law, so we watch without touching. It is read at Easter, the spring holiday of new life, when eggs are a sign of what is about to hatch.

excerpt.locator: Garden Days, II, “Nest Eggs,” the complete poem; opens “BIRDS all the sunny day Flutter and quarrel Here in the arbour-like Tent of the laurel.”; closes “In spite of our wisdom And sensible talking, We on our feet must go Plodding and walking.”.

questions.prompt: How many eggs are in the nest, and what colour are they?
facilitatorNotes: Four little blue eggs, which the mother keeps warm.
evidence: Four little blue eggs
The mother keeps heated.

questions.prompt: What will the baby birds do soon after they hatch?
facilitatorNotes: Chip their way out and fill the April woods with singing, then fly into the blue air.
evidence: Merry with singing.
Soon in blue air they'll be,

questions.prompt: The children are older and stronger. Why will they no longer “look down” on the birds?
facilitatorNotes: The birds will fly high in the beeches while the children must walk. Being bigger does not let them fly; some children hear the speaker as a little envious, others as happy for the birds.
evidence: We shall look down on the Birdies no longer.
We on our feet must go

readings.title: The Flowers
readings.challenge: Hear real flower names and imagine the tiny world they suggest.
readings.focus: Old country names for flowers make a child picture a fairy forest at his feet.
readings.context: Gardener's garters, shepherd's purse, bachelor's buttons, lady's smock and hollyhock are real names of flowers and plants that grow in Britain. Dames are ladies; boughs are branches; thyme is a small sweet-smelling herb. Read the names slowly, as if each one were a treasure.

excerpt.locator: Garden Days, III, “The Flowers,” the complete poem; opens “ALL the names I know from nurse: Gardener's garters, Shepherd's purse, Bachelor's…”; closes “…fairest woods are these; Where, if I were not so tall, I should live for good and all.”.

questions.prompt: Who taught the child the flower names? Which name do you like best?
facilitatorNotes: His nurse. Any name counts; ask what it makes the child picture.
evidence: ALL the names I know from nurse:

questions.prompt: Why does the child decide these must be “fairy names”?
facilitatorNotes: They sound like things that belong to people, garters, a purse, buttons, a smock, yet the flowers are tiny, so he imagines tiny people own them.
evidence: These must all be fairy names!
Tiny trees for tiny dames--

questions.prompt: Why would the child like to live in these woods “for good and all,” and what stops him?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks they are the fairest woods of all, but he is too tall to fit. Children may say they would like to be small too, or that it would be scary down there; either can come from the poem.
evidence: But the fairest woods are these;
Where, if I were not so tall,

readings.title: The Dumb Soldier
readings.challenge: Imagine what a toy has seen while nobody was watching.
readings.focus: A toy soldier hidden in the lawn all spring has seen the whole small world of the grass, but cannot tell it.
readings.context: Dumb here means unable to speak. A grenadier is a kind of soldier; old toy soldiers were made of lead, so his eyes are leaden. A scythe is a long curved blade for cutting grass, and stoning it means sharpening it on a stone. Disclose means tell.

excerpt.locator: Garden Days, V, “The Dumb Soldier,” the complete poem; opens “WHEN the grass was closely mown, Walking on the lawn alone, In the turf a hole I found…”; closes “…Not a word of all he knows. I must lay him on the shelf, And make up the tale myself.”.

questions.prompt: Where does the child hide the toy soldier, and why can’t he find him for a while?
facilitatorNotes: In a hole in the freshly mown lawn. Then the spring grass grows tall and covers the hiding place until the lawn is cut again.
evidence: And hid a soldier underground.
Grasses hide my hiding place;

questions.prompt: What might the soldier have seen and heard down in the grass?
facilitatorNotes: The starry nights, the flowers coming up, fairy things passing, bees and ladybirds talking, and a butterfly flying over. Children can pick one and describe it.
evidence: And the springing of the flowers;
Talking bee and ladybird,

questions.prompt: The soldier will not say a word. What will the child do instead?
facilitatorNotes: Put him on the shelf and make up the story himself. The poem ends with the child’s imagination doing what the toy cannot. Ask what story the child would invent for the soldier.
evidence: Not a word will he disclose,
And make up the tale myself.

readings.title: The Gardener
readings.challenge: Compare how the gardener spends the summer with how the child wants him to spend it.
readings.focus: A child cannot understand a grown-up who works instead of playing, and warns him that summer will end.
readings.context: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these poems as if a child were speaking. The gravel walk is a path of small stones; currants are small berries; plots are garden beds; a barrow is a wheelbarrow; to profit by something means to make the most of it.
readings.contentNote: The child wants to play “Indian wars,” a pretend fighting game of Stevenson’s time in which American Indians were the enemy.

excerpt.locator: Garden Days, VII, “The Gardener,” the complete poem; opens “THE gardener does not love to talk, He makes me keep the gravel walk; And when he puts…”; closes “…by these garden days, O how much wiser you would be To play at Indian wars with me!”.

questions.prompt: What does the gardener do all day, and what does he not want to do?
facilitatorNotes: He keeps the paths, locks up his tools, digs the flower beds and cuts the hay; he does not want to talk or play.
evidence: THE gardener does not love to talk,
And never seems to want to play.

questions.prompt: The child calls him “Silly gardener!” What does he warn him about?
facilitatorNotes: Summer will end and winter will come, so the gardener will have to put his barrow away; the child thinks he should play while summer lasts.
evidence: And winter comes with pinching toes,
You must lay your barrow down.

questions.prompt: Who do you think is wiser, the child or the gardener? Use the poem.
facilitatorNotes: The child says playing would be wiser. But the same fact, that summer is short, explains why the gardener is so busy: summer is when the garden needs him. Children may side with either; ask each to give a line.
evidence: O how much wiser you would be
He digs the flowers and cuts the hay,
